report_title: Volatile Cedar / Lebanese Cedar (Explosive RAT) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: Check Point Software 'Volatile Cedar — Analysis of a Global Cyber Espionage Campaign' technical report (2015-03-30, https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2015/03/20082004/volatile-cedar-technical-report.pdf ; https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/volatilecedar/); ClearSky Cyber Security '"Lebanese Cedar" APT — Global Lebanese Espionage Campaign Leveraging Web Servers' (2021-01, https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Lebanese-Cedar-APT.pdf ; https://www.clearskysec.com/cedar/); Kaspersky Securelist 'Sinkholing Volatile Cedar DGA Infrastructure' (2015, https://securelist.com/sinkholing-volatile-cedar-dga-infrastructure/69421/). Public MITRE ATT&CK Group id G0123 (Volatile Cedar) cited as reference only.

actor.name: Volatile Cedar
aliases: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0123 (public MITRE reference only)
related_clusters: Explosive RAT operators (the only known APT to use the Explosive RAT codebase, v1 through v4)
actor.attribution: Lebanon-nexus cyber-espionage actor, assessed with medium-to-high confidence to be linked to the Lebanese political/militant group Hezbollah. Check Point (2015) attributed the campaign to a persistent, well-organized group with a 'possible link to a Lebanese political group' based on operational security discipline, target selection aligned with Lebanese/Hezbollah geopolitical interests, and Arabic-language artifacts; ClearSky (2021) reinforced the Hezbollah linkage. Attribution is analytic (based on victimology, TTP continuity and language artifacts) rather than proven by hard technical indicators; it is not a formal government attribution, so it is treated as medium-high, not high.
targeted_regions_global: Worldwide (250+ internet-facing servers breached across multiple regions)

key_campaigns.name: Volatile Cedar (original Explosive RAT campaign)
key_campaigns.summary: Long-running, low-profile cyber-espionage campaign. Initial access achieved by attacking public-facing web servers via vulnerability scanning and SQL injection, then dropping a JSP web shell used to reconnoiter the target and implant the custom Explosive RAT. Explosive (main binary + separate API DLL, versions 1.x–3.x) provided keylogging, screenshot capture, HTTP command-and-control, and self-update. The group deliberately kept a small footprint, patched the implant to evade heuristic AV, and used static updater C2 servers that fell back to a DGA when hardcoded C2 was unreachable.

key_campaigns.name: Lebanese Cedar 2020–2021 resurgence (Explosive v4 / Caterpillar WebShell)
key_campaigns.summary: Resurgent global espionage campaign disclosed by ClearSky. The group exploited known 1-day vulnerabilities on unpatched internet-facing Atlassian (Confluence CVE-2019-3396, Jira CVE-2019-11581) and Oracle 10g (CVE-2012-3152) servers, deploying the Caterpillar WebShell (a modified JSP file-browser based on the ASPXSpy web shell) and, on many hosts, the fourth version of the Explosive RAT. ClearSky identified ~250 breached servers, primarily at telecommunications companies and ISPs/hosting providers across the US, UK, Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Jordan, UAE and the Palestinian Authority. Explosive v4 added evasion via obfuscation, communication encryption, and a separate DLL for API activity, and used hardcoded static C2 plus DGA-based dynamic update servers.

malware: Explosive RAT (custom, versions 1.x, 2.x, 3.x and 4.x; main binary + separate API DLL)
Caterpillar WebShell (modified JSP file-browser, based on the ASPXSpy web shell)
tooling_observed: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group

ttps.procedure_description: Actors scan internet-facing web servers for exploitable weaknesses (SQL-injectable parameters and known-vulnerable Atlassian/Oracle software versions) as the front of their public-web-server intrusion model. ClearSky observed selection of unpatched Confluence, Jira and Oracle 10g servers, indicating version/vulnerability probing at scale (~250 servers breached).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — vulnerability probing of internet-facing servers happens off-victim at the perimeter and rarely attributes cleanly to this actor; hunt/intel candidate via external attack-surface monitoring and WAF/edge scan-pattern review

ttps.procedure_description: Actors sweep internet IP space to discover exposed web/application servers running vulnerable Atlassian and Oracle products before targeting them, consistent with the opportunistic, internet-wide server-selection model described by both Check Point and ClearSky.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim internet scanning is not endpoint-observable; intel/hunt candidate only

ttps.procedure_description: The group develops and maintains its own custom Explosive RAT codebase (versions 1.x through 4.x) — it is the only known APT to use Explosive. The RAT is deliberately split into a main binary and a separate DLL so operators can quickly patch/update functionality and evade heuristic detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — malware development occurs off-victim; intel candidate. Detection lands on the deployed implant's host/network behaviors, not its development

ttps.procedure_description: Actors register and operate hardcoded static updater C2 domains (e.g. edortntexplore[.]info) plus a pool of DGA-generated domains used as dynamic update servers for Explosive fallback communications.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — adversary domain registration is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via infrastructure tracking and passive DNS. On-victim detection is via resolution/connection to these domains (see C2 techniques)

ttps.procedure_description: Signature initial-access vector: compromise of public-facing web/application servers. In the original campaign this was primarily SQL injection against vulnerable web servers; in the 2020–2021 resurgence the group exploited known 1-day vulnerabilities on unpatched internet-facing Atlassian Confluence (CVE-2019-3396), Atlassian Jira (CVE-2019-11581) and Oracle 10g (CVE-2012-3152) servers to gain code execution and plant a web shell.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — exploitation of these specific CVEs and SQLi on internet-facing Atlassian/Oracle servers is a strong detection surface: WAF/exploit signatures, anomalous requests to vulnerable endpoints, web-server error/access logs, and post-exploit child processes spawned by the web/app server (java/w3wp spawning cmd) plus version/patch-state monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: After exploiting a public-facing server, actors drop a JSP web shell and, in the 2020–2021 campaign, the Caterpillar WebShell — a modified JSP file-browser derived from the ASPXSpy web shell — to maintain access, browse the filesystem, run commands and stage the Explosive implant. The web shell was found on the majority of investigated victims (~250 breached servers).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — web-shell files (Caterpillar/ASPXSpy-derived JSP, modified file-browser) written into Atlassian/Oracle/IIS web roots are detectable via file-integrity monitoring, web-shell YARA/signature scanning, and anomalous POSTs to newly created server-side script files; the web/app-server process spawning command interpreters is a further high-fidelity signal

ttps.procedure_description: Actors run operating-system commands through the deployed web shell (and via the Explosive implant) to enumerate the host and network and to install/execute further tooling on the compromised server.
observed_tooling: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — command execution spawned by a web/application-server process (java, w3wp, tomcat) is detectable via process-lineage telemetry, but the individual commands are common and need parent-process context

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive is architected as a main binary plus a separate DLL that provides its API/functionality; the loader binary loads this companion module at runtime, letting operators patch the DLL independently to update capability and dodge heuristic detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the main-binary-plus-companion-DLL load pattern is observable via module-load (image-load) telemetry when the DLL is unsigned/anomalous, but requires a known-bad DLL or path baseline

ttps.procedure_description: The Explosive implant relies on a paired DLL for its core API activity, loaded by the main binary; this modular DLL design is used both for functionality and to keep the malicious code in a separately updatable module that can be swapped to evade signature detection. (Env note: mapped to T1574.001 'DLL'; T1574.002 side-loading is absent in this dataset.)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — an unsigned/unusual companion DLL loaded from the same directory as the Explosive main binary is detectable via image-load and signature-mismatch telemetry, but the RAT does not clearly abuse a signed host binary, so confidence is moderate

ttps.procedure_description: Operators run ipconfig (and equivalent commands) via the web shell to map the compromised host's network configuration and identify reachable segments.
observed_tooling: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — ipconfig is benign in isolation; suspicious when spawned by a web-server process in a short recon burst — detectable via command-line + parent-process correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Operators run whoami via the web shell to determine the security context/privileges of the compromised service account.
observed_tooling: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami executed as a child of a web/app-server process is a recognizable post-exploitation recon signal via process-lineage telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Operators run net group commands via the web shell to enumerate domain groups and identify privileged accounts/high-value targets within the compromised environment.
observed_tooling: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'net group /domain' spawned by a web-server process is detectable via command-line logging with parent-process context; common admin tool otherwise

ttps.procedure_description: The web shell and Explosive implant gather host information (OS, hostname, system details) to profile the compromised server and tailor follow-on activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — host enumeration is common; meaningful mainly inside a web-shell-driven recon burst

ttps.procedure_description: Actors use the Caterpillar WebShell's file-browser functionality to enumerate the filesystem of the compromised server, locating configuration files, credentials and data of interest.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — file/directory browsing via a web shell is detectable through the web shell's own request patterns and web-server access logs, but blends with legitimate file access absent web-shell context

ttps.procedure_description: After establishing a foothold on a public-facing server, operators enumerate other reachable internal hosts to plan lateral movement toward high-value systems.
observed_tooling: Windows built-ins: ipconfig, whoami, net group
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal host enumeration is detectable via command-line logging and connection-fanout analytics, but is common admin behavior

ttps.procedure_description: The Explosive RAT includes a keylogging capability, capturing keystrokes on the compromised host and exfiltrating them to the C2 for credential and intelligence collection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — keylogging is detectable via API-hook/keyboard-hook behavioral telemetry and the RAT's process/C2 behavior, but the keylogging primitive itself leaves limited discrete host signal without EDR behavioral analytics

ttps.procedure_description: The Explosive RAT can capture screenshots of the victim's desktop and send them to the C2 as part of its surveillance/collection functionality.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — screen-capture API usage by an untrusted process is detectable via EDR behavioral telemetry; corroborated by the RAT's distinctive C2, but not high-fidelity on its own

ttps.procedure_description: Operators collect files and data of interest from the compromised server/host, both via the Caterpillar WebShell file-browser and via the Explosive implant, for espionage exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — local data collection is common; suspicious mainly via staging patterns and web-shell/RAT process context

ttps.procedure_description: Captured keystrokes, screenshots and collected files are staged locally on the compromised host prior to HTTP exfiltration to the Explosive C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — local staging of small espionage artifacts leaves little discrete signal; hunt candidate via file-write telemetry in RAT working directories

ttps.procedure_description: Post-exploitation, operators harvest credentials from compromised hosts to enable lateral movement and pass-the-hash across the network.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — credential harvesting/dumping is detectable via process-access to credential stores and known-tool signatures, but the reports do not name the specific dumping tool, lowering fidelity

ttps.technique_name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
ttps.procedure_description: Operators reuse harvested credential material (hashes) to authenticate to additional systems and traverse network segments after compromising the initial public-facing server.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — pass-the-hash is detectable via NTLM Type-3 logon anomalies and mismatched credential-source analytics, but is subtle and blends with admin activity

ttps.procedure_description: Operators use PsExec (SMB/admin-share remote execution) to run code on additional hosts and move laterally within the compromised environment.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — PsExec service creation and ADMIN$/C$ access are detectable via remote service-install (Event ID 7045), 5140 share access and Type-3 logons, but PsExec is also legitimately used by admins

ttps.procedure_description: Operators move the Explosive implant and supporting tooling from the initially compromised web server to other internal hosts during lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal SMB/admin-share file transfers of executables are detectable via file-write-over-network and share-access telemetry, but require east-west visibility

ttps.procedure_description: The Explosive RAT communicates with its command-and-control servers over HTTP(S). Beacons use a distinctive/hardcoded HTTP User-Agent and structured URI pattern (e.g. Kaspersky observed check-ins to the static C2 edortntexplore[.]info at URI /micro/data/index.php?micro=4 over port 443), providing a recognizable network signature.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — the RAT's HTTP beaconing with a distinctive User-Agent and fixed URI structure to known C2 hosts is a strong network-detection surface via proxy/DNS/IDS signatures and JA3/UA anomaly analytics (exact User-Agent string not asserted here as it was not verifiable from a primary source)

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive uses hardcoded static updater C2 servers as its primary channel; when the implant cannot reach its hardcoded static C2, it falls back to a DGA and cycles through dynamically generated domains to re-establish communications.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — fallback behavior manifests as bursts of failed connections followed by resolution of algorithmic domains, detectable via DNS/NX-domain analytics, but requires baselining

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive's control network includes DGA-based dynamic update servers; when the static/hardcoded C2 is unavailable the implant algorithmically generates candidate domains to locate live infrastructure (the DGA infrastructure was sinkholed by Kaspersky).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — DGA beaconing is detectable via DNS analytics (high-entropy domain names, NXDOMAIN bursts, algorithmic patterns), though generic DGA detection needs tuning to this family

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive includes a self-update mechanism: it retrieves updated binaries/DLLs from static and DGA-based update servers, letting operators refresh the implant to add functionality and evade detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — implant self-update pulls executable content from C2/update servers, detectable via proxy file-download + subsequent binary-replacement telemetry when the update endpoints are known/blocklisted

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive v4 encrypts its command-and-control communications (one of several evasion techniques ClearSky attributes to the RAT) to hinder network inspection and content-based detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — payload encryption defeats content inspection; detection shifts to metadata/beacon-cadence and known C2 endpoints rather than the encryption itself (hunt-leaning)

ttps.procedure_description: Explosive employs obfuscation to hinder analysis and evade heuristic AV detection; combined with the modular main-binary/DLL split, operators repeatedly re-obfuscate and patch the implant to stay ahead of signatures.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — obfuscation reduces static-signature efficacy; detection relies on behavioral/dynamic analysis rather than the obfuscation itself (hunt-leaning)

ttps.procedure_description: The Explosive implant decodes/decrypts its obfuscated components and C2 payloads at runtime to execute functionality, complementing its static obfuscation and communication encryption.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — runtime deobfuscation is internal to the process and hard to observe directly; hunt candidate via memory/behavioral analysis

detection_signals: Exploitation attempts and post-exploit activity against internet-facing Atlassian Confluence (CVE-2019-3396), Atlassian Jira (CVE-2019-11581) and Oracle 10g (CVE-2012-3152), plus SQL-injection probing of public web servers — WAF/exploit signatures, web-server access/error logs and version/patch-state monitoring

Web-shell files written into web application roots: Caterpillar WebShell / ASPXSpy-derived modified-JSP file-browser on Atlassian/Oracle/IIS servers — file-integrity monitoring and web-shell YARA/signature scanning
Web/application-server processes (java, tomcat, w3wp) spawning command interpreters and running ipconfig / whoami / net group in a short recon burst
Explosive RAT beaconing over HTTP(S) with a distinctive/hardcoded User-Agent and fixed URI pattern (e.g. /micro/data/index.php?micro=4) to known static C2
DNS resolution of or connections to the static updater C2 edortntexplore[.]info and to the Explosive C2 IPs (68.65.122.109, 74.208.73.149, 191.101.5.183, 198.101.242.72, 169.50.13.61)
DGA fallback behavior: NXDOMAIN bursts followed by resolution of high-entropy algorithmically generated domains when hardcoded C2 is unreachable
A main-binary plus companion API-DLL load pattern where the DLL is unsigned/anomalous; implant self-update pulling executables from update servers
PsExec-based remote execution and pass-the-hash lateral movement from an initially compromised public-facing server (Event ID 7045, Type-3 NTLM logons)
Presence of any of the Explosive RAT or Caterpillar/ASPXSpy web-shell MD5 hashes listed in the IOCs section on web servers or endpoints
notes: Primary sources: Check Point 'Volatile Cedar' technical report (2015) and ClearSky '"Lebanese Cedar" APT' report (Jan 2021), enriched with Kaspersky Securelist's DGA-sinkholing article (2015). This is the FIRST Lebanon-cluster pack in the library. Attribution is Lebanon-nexus / assessed-Hezbollah-linked at MEDIUM-HIGH confidence: it is an analytic vendor assessment based on victimology, TTP/tooling continuity (exclusive use of Explosive RAT) and language artifacts, not a formal government attribution — hence not 'high'. actor.mitre_id intentionally left empty per tasking; public MITRE Group id G0123 (Volatile Cedar) is cited as an alias/reference only. ENV MAPPING NOTES: every technique_id was validated as a key in this environment's bundled attack_dump.json (697 techniques) before inclusion — zero invalid IDs. Defense-evasion techniques use the env tactic slug 'stealth' (T1027, T1140). The Explosive modular main-binary/DLL design is mapped to T1129 (Shared Modules, execution) and T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL) rather than T1574.002 side-loading, which is absent from this dataset; note the RAT is modular by design rather than a classic signed-host side-load, so those two entries carry medium (not high) feasibility. IOC INTEGRITY NOTE: an initial WebFetch parse of the ClearSky PDF binary returned obviously fabricated placeholder indicators (round-number hashes, an implausible 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows; custom RAT)' User-Agent, and fake domains malware-command[.]ru / exfil-data[.]cc) — these were REJECTED as hallucinations and are NOT in this pack. The IOCs included here are the real MD5 sample/webshell hashes, C2 IPs and the static C2 domain edortntexplore[.]info drawn from the reports' appendices as reproduced by readable secondary sources (ClearSky IOC appendix and Kaspersky Securelist), normalized to lowercase and un-defanged for machine use. No Explosive RAT User-Agent string is asserted because it could not be verified from a primary source (the fetched value was fabricated); the distinctive-UA behavior is captured as a TTP/detection signal without a specific string. DETECTION SURFACE (detect-candidate, high feasibility): T1190 Atlassian/Oracle CVE + SQLi exploitation on internet-facing servers; T1505.003 Caterpillar/ASPXSpy web shells in web roots; T1071.001 Explosive HTTP C2 with distinctive UA/URI to known C2. HUNT-leaning (low feasibility, off-victim or evasion-internal): T1595.x scanning, T1587.001/T1583.001 malware+infra development, T1573 encrypted C2, T1027/T1140 obfuscation/deobfuscation, T1074.001 local staging.
